title: The Voyages of Christopher Columbus
intro: Between 1492 and 1504 the Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus led four transatlantic expeditions in the name of the Catholic Monarchs of Spain. He sailed in search of a westward route to India, China, Japan and the Spice Islands, and believed at first that he had reached the Indies.
ending: After the fourth voyage Columbus reached Spain in November 1504 and died in 1506. The Americas were already inhabited by Indigenous peoples, and his voyages led to the Spanish colonization and conquest that followed.

stops.text: Columbus set out with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, going down the Rio Tinto into the Atlantic.
stops.quote: On the morning of 3 August 1492, the expedition departed from the Port of Palos, going down the Rio Tinto and into the Atlantic.

stops.text: After repairs to the Pinta's rudder in the Canary Islands, the ships met at La Gomera and departed from there for the Atlantic crossing, which lasted five weeks.
stops.quote: on 6 September the ships departed San Sebastián de La Gomera for what turned out to be a five-week-long westward voyage across the Atlantic.

stops.text: Columbus came ashore on an island he called San Salvador, known to its people as Guanahani. He thought he had reached the Indies, and he met the Lucayan, Taíno and Arawak peoples and took some Arawaks prisoner.
stops.quote: Columbus called this island San Salvador; its Indigenous name was Guanahani. The modern San Salvador Island in the Bahamas is considered to be the most likely candidate for this island.

stops.text: Columbus landed on the eastern coast of a large island he called Juana and explored its northeast coast. He believed he was near the lands of Asia.
stops.quote: Subsequently they headed toward the eastern coast of a large island which they called Juana (present-day Cuba), landing there on 28 October 1492.

stops.text: The Santa María ran aground on Hispaniola on 25 December and was abandoned. Columbus began a fort built from its remains and left 39 men there.
stops.quote: Fort Navidad, built with the remains of the Santa María in works that began on 26 December 1492.

stops.text: On the way home the Niña anchored off the island, where the cable broke on rocks. The island's captain later held part of the crew prisoner for a time.
stops.quote: On the night of 17 February, the Niña laid anchor at Santa Maria Island, but the cable broke on sharp rocks, forcing Columbus to stay offshore until morning when a safer location was found nearby.

stops.text: A storm forced Columbus into Lisbon. King John II of Portugal met him and said he believed the voyage broke the 1479 Treaty of Alcáçovas.
stops.quote: Leaving the island of Santa Maria in the Azores on 23 February, Columbus headed for Castilian Spain, but another storm forced him into Lisbon. He anchored next to a king's harbor patrol ship on 4 March 1493, where he was told a fleet of 100 caravels had been lost in the storm.

stops.text: Columbus arrived back at his starting port and later reported to Ferdinand and Isabella in Barcelona, bringing gold samples, plants and some Taíno he had kidnapped.
stops.quote: He arrived back in Palos on 15 March 1493 and later met with Ferdinand and Isabella in Barcelona to report his findings.

stops.text: Columbus sailed with a much larger fleet of two carracks and 15 caravels. The stated purpose was to convert the Indigenous Americans to Christianity.
stops.quote: He set sail from Cádiz, Spain, on 25 September 1493.

stops.text: The fleet landed on a rugged shore of this island, which Columbus named Dominica. On the same day he landed at Marie-Galante.
stops.quote: On 3 November 1493, Christopher Columbus landed on a rugged shore on an island that he named Dominica.

stops.text: The fleet sighted the island, known to the Taíno as Borinquen, on 17 November and landed at the Bay of Añasco on 19 November. Columbus named it San Juan Bautista and stayed two days.
stops.quote: The fleet continued to the Greater Antilles, first sighting the eastern coast of the island of Puerto Rico, known to the native Taíno people as Borinquen, on the afternoon of 17 November 1493. The fleet sailed along the island's southern coast for a whole day, before making landfall on its northwestern coast at the Bay of Añasco, between the modern towns of Mayagüez and Aguadilla, early on 19 November 1493.

stops.text: The fleet signalled the fort and got no answer. Next day the Spaniards found its burnt remains, and Guacanagari's cousin admitted that Caonabo had wiped out the Europeans.
stops.quote: On the night of 27 November, cannons and flares were ignited in an attempt to signal La Navidad, but there was no response. A canoe party led by a cousin of Guacanagari presented Columbus with two golden masks and told him that Guacanagari had been injured by another chief, Caonabo, and that except for some Spanish casualties resulting from sickness and quarrel, the rest of his men were well. The next day, the Spanish fleet discovered the burnt remains of the Navidad fortress, and Guacanagari's cousin admitted that the Europeans had been wiped out by Caonabo.

stops.text: The fleet reached a plain on the north coast of Hispaniola and founded the settlement of La Isabela. By the end of 1494 disease and famine had claimed two-thirds of the Spanish settlers.
stops.quote: arriving at a plain on the north coast of Hispaniola on 2 January 1494. There, they established the settlement of La Isabela.

stops.text: After leaving Hispaniola, Columbus reached Cuba on 30 April and Discovery Bay on 5 May. He then explored the south coast of Cuba, which he believed to be a peninsula of China.
stops.quote: Columbus left Hispaniola on 24 April 1494, and arrived at the island of Cuba (which he had named Juana during his first voyage) on 30 April and Discovery Bay, Jamaica, on 5 May.

stops.text: Short of food on the way home, Columbus asked the people of Guadeloupe for supplies. They ambushed the Spaniards with arrows, who destroyed some huts and held 13 women and children hostage to force a sale of cassava.
stops.quote: on 10 April, Columbus requested food from the Natives of Guadeloupe. Upon going ashore, the Spaniards were ambushed by arrows; in response, they destroyed some huts. They then held a group of 13 native women and children hostage to force a sale of cassava.

stops.text: After landing in Portugal near Odemira on 8 June, the fleet returned to Spain through the Bay of Cádiz.
stops.quote: On 8 June, the fleet landed at Portugal, near Odemira, and returned to Spain via the Bay of Cádiz on 11 June.

stops.text: Columbus left with six ships. Three went straight to Hispaniola with supplies, while he took the other three to explore what lay to the south.
stops.quote: On 30 May 1498, Columbus left with six ships from Sanlúcar, Spain, for his third trip to the Americas.

stops.text: The fleet sighted Trinidad from the southeast, sailed along its southern coast and anchored near Soldado Rock, where it met a group of Amerindians in canoes.
stops.quote: The men sighted the land of Trinidad on 31 July, approaching from the southeast.

stops.text: After crossing the Gulf of Paria, the fleet landed on the mainland of South America. Columbus called it another world but still believed it was Asia.
stops.quote: The men sailed across the Gulf of Paria, and on 5 August, landed on the mainland of South America at the Paria Peninsula.

stops.text: Columbus sailed to the islands of Chacachacare and Margarita. He also sighted Tobago and Grenada.
stops.quote: He then sailed to the islands of Chacachacare and Margarita (reaching the latter on 14 August), and sighted Tobago (which he named Bella Forma) and Grenada (which he named Concepción).

stops.text: Columbus returned in poor health to find many of the settlers in rebellion against his rule. They said he had misled them about the riches they expected.
stops.quote: In poor health, Columbus returned to Hispaniola on 19 August, only to find that many of the Spanish settlers of the new colony were in rebellion against his rule, claiming that Columbus had misled them about the supposedly bountiful riches they expected to find.

stops.text: Columbus came back to Santo Domingo planning to sail to Spain to answer the rebels' accounts. In 1500 the Crown had him removed as governor and sent to Spain in chains.
stops.quote: On 3 February 1500, he returned to Santo Domingo with plans to sail back to Spain to defend himself from the accounts of the rebels.

stops.text: The king and queen summoned the Columbus brothers to the Alhambra. With his chains removed, Columbus admitted his faults and begged forgiveness, and their freedom was restored.
stops.quote: On 12 December 1500, the king and queen summoned the Columbus brothers to their presence at the Alhambra palace in Granada.

stops.text: Columbus left with four ships, seeking a westward passage to the Indian Ocean. The king and queen ordered him not to stop at Hispaniola.
stops.quote: he left Cádiz on 9 May 1502, with his flagship, Capitana, as well as the Gallega, Vizcaína, and Santiago de Palos.

stops.text: After a crossing of twenty days with the trade winds, the ships landed at Carbet on Martinique.
stops.quote: on 15 June, they landed at Carbet on the island of Martinique (Martinica).

stops.text: Columbus expected a hurricane and asked for shelter. He was refused port, and the governor would not heed his warning. A storm then sank many ships, and some of his enemies accused him of conjuring it.
stops.quote: He arrived at Santo Domingo on June 29, but was denied port, and the new governor refused to listen to his warning of a storm.

stops.text: Columbus reached the Bay Islands off Honduras. His brother Bartolomeo found native merchants, possibly Mayans, in a large canoe, and the local people introduced Columbus to cacao.
stops.quote: he sailed to modern Central America, arriving at Guanaja (Isla de los Pinos) in the Bay Islands off the coast of Honduras on 30 July 1502.

stops.text: After two months searching the coasts of Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica for a passage, Columbus arrived in Almirante Bay in Panama.
stops.quote: He spent two months exploring the coasts of Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica looking for the passage, before arriving in Almirante Bay, Panama, on 16 October.

stops.text: Columbus set up a garrison at the river's mouth after hearing from the Ngobe of gold and a strait to another ocean. The local leader El Quibían later attacked, and one ship had to be abandoned.
stops.quote: In Panamá, he learned from the Ngobe of gold and a strait to another ocean. After some exploration, he established a garrison at the mouth of Belén River in January 1503.

stops.text: Damaged by storms, the ships were beached in Jamaica, where Columbus and his men remained stranded for a year. Help came from Hispaniola on 29 June 1504.
stops.quote: Unable to travel any farther, the ships were beached in St. Ann's Bay, Jamaica, on 25 June.

stops.text: Columbus and his son Fernando had left Hispaniola in a caravel on 11 September 1504. They arrived at Sanlúcar and travelled on to Seville.
stops.quote: They arrived in Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 7 November and from there they traveled to Seville.

notes: Left out (8-per-leg limit or nothing happened): Samaná Peninsula / Bay of Arrows (13 January 1493), Saint Croix (14 November 1493, a violent encounter with Carib people), Odemira, Madeira and Porto Santo (no dates), Puerto Castilla, Cuba 1494 (folded into the Jamaica stop). Cuba and Puerto Rico wp titles are the whole-island/territory articles; the editor may prefer a coastal point. Granada is reached by land only by inference (the article names no route, and says Columbus was in Cádiz first); wp is the Alhambra. La Navidad 1493: 27 November is the night of the signalling, the discovery of the ruins is 'the next day'. Trinidad entry left null (the places.tsv Trinidad is unverified); Almirante Bay and Belén River titles are best guesses. San Salvador is the article's 'most likely' identification of Guanahani; the 12 October date comes from the landing section, not from the quoted sentences. Cape Verde Islands appear in the article only in passing.
